title: Three lines: planning, avoidance and evasion
summary: Reducing tax sits on a line that runs from ordinary planning, through avoidance, to evasion. Planning uses the law as intended, avoidance uses its letter against its purpose, and evasion breaks it by concealment or falsehood. Knowing where a proposal sits, and why, is a core skill for any developer.
body:
Mr Shabazz, there are three ways to pay less tax, and only one of them is safe to build a career on. Planning uses the law as it was meant to be used. Avoidance uses the letter of the law against its purpose and invites challenge. Evasion breaks the law by hiding or lying, and it is a crime.

Recall

Q. What is recapture, in concept?

A. Recapture is the clawing back, on a sale, of tax depreciation previously deducted, where the sale price shows the asset did not lose the value the deductions assumed. It is often taxed differently from the gain above original cost.

Q. What is the difference between residence and source taxation?

A. Residence taxation is based on who the taxpayer is and usually reaches worldwide income. Source taxation is based on where income arises. Land is taxed heavily at source because it cannot move.

Q. Name the three classic approaches to valuing property.

A. The income approach, the sales comparison approach and the cost approach. Each answers the question of value from a different direction, and an appraiser reconciles them.

Why this matters

Tax is often the largest single cost a developer can influence after land and construction. That makes it the area where you will be offered the most clever ideas, by advisers, promoters, partners and contractors. Some of those ideas are sound. Some will cost you more than they save once the authority reviews them. A few will expose you to penalties or prosecution. You need a way to sort them quickly, before you have committed money, and a vocabulary that lets you ask the right questions. Cole joins me this week because the line between these categories is usually decided by evidence. All of this is concept, not advice; no rate, penalty or rule here should be relied on without verifying it against the primary source and with a qualified adviser in each country.

The three categories

In plain English: tax planning is choosing, among options the law offers, the one that costs least. Holding an investment property long term rather than flipping it, claiming the depreciation the law allows, or timing a sale into a later year are ordinary planning. The law expects people to make these choices.

Tax avoidance means arranging transactions so that they fall within the literal words of a tax rule while defeating the purpose of that rule. The transactions are real and disclosed, but they exist mainly to produce a tax result the legislature did not intend. Avoidance is generally not a crime. It is, however, exactly what anti-avoidance rules are written to attack, and when they apply the authority can recharacterise the transaction and deny the benefit, often with interest, and in some systems with penalties.

Tax evasion means illegally reducing tax by concealment, false statements or deliberate failure to report: hiding income, inventing expenses, under-declaring a sale price, or keeping cash sales off the books. It is a criminal offence in most systems, and the penalties can include fines and imprisonment as well as the tax itself.

Notice that evasion does not need a complicated structure. It can be one false line on a return, one invoice that was never issued, or one sale price written lower than the price actually paid. And it can make other people parties to it: the buyer who signs a deed showing a false price, or the developer who accepts an unrecorded cash discount, may share the exposure even though the idea was someone else's.

The professional framing is a single question for each category. For planning: is this the choice the law offers? For avoidance: does this use a rule in a way its purpose would reject? For evasion: does this depend on the authority not knowing the true facts? If any part of a proposal only works if the authority does not find out, it is not planning.

Say that out loud now.

Substance over form

Legal systems take different views on how far tax follows the legal form of a transaction rather than its economic substance. Some courts start from the legal form, so that a transaction documented as a sale is treated as a sale, and leave it to specific statutory rules to override that. Others give more weight to what the transaction does in economic terms. Most modern systems combine the two: they respect legal form in general, and they add anti-avoidance rules that let the authority look at substance when a transaction is abusive.

There are two kinds of anti-avoidance rule. A specific anti-avoidance rule targets a known technique, for example rules restricting the use of losses after a change of control. A general anti-avoidance rule, often called a GAAR, is a broad provision that lets the authority deny a tax benefit from a transaction whose main purpose is tax and which misuses or abuses the purpose of the provisions relied on. Canada has had a GAAR since 1988; many countries have one now, and they are amended from time to time. Verify the current text and its tests against the primary source before relying on any of it.

Two developer examples

First, hypothetical, a land transfer. A developer wants to buy land worth 10,000,000 in a jurisdiction that charges a hypothetical 3 percent transfer tax on land transfers, or 300,000. The seller holds the land in a company that owns nothing else. Buying the shares rather than the land may not trigger the land transfer tax under that jurisdiction's rules. Is that planning or avoidance? It depends on the rules. Many jurisdictions have rules that treat a transfer of shares in a land-rich company as a transfer of land precisely to stop this. Where such a rule exists, the share purchase may simply be taxed. Where none exists, a share purchase made for genuine commercial reasons, such as keeping existing contracts and approvals in place, may be ordinary planning. The facts and the statute decide, and the purchaser also inherits the company's history, including its tax history.

Second, hypothetical, a contractor offer. A contractor offers a 5 percent discount on a 2,000,000 fit-out contract if you pay part of it in cash, without an invoice. This is not a grey area. The contractor is proposing to keep income off his books and to avoid charging sales tax, and you would be asked to keep an expense off yours. It is evasion, and by agreeing you would be party to it. Decline, and record that you declined.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not evasion, which most honest developers recognise. It is avoidance sold as planning by someone who is paid when you agree. The control is a three-line test written into your approval process for any tax proposal: state the non-tax commercial purpose in one sentence, confirm the plan works if the authority sees every document, and require a written opinion from an independent adviser who is not paid on the size of the saving. Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser in each relevant country, and a lawyer where the plan changes legal ownership.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a plan is safe because it is legal on the words of the statute. Avoidance always looks legal on the words. That is what makes it avoidance. The question is whether it survives the purpose test, and that question is answered by courts years later, on the evidence you created at the time.

Callback

In week 22 you met Fundy Settlement, where a trust's address said one country and its decisions said another. That case was about residence, but it shared the core lesson of this week: tax authorities and courts look at what actually happened, not at what the documents claim. And in week 21, courts pierced the corporate veil only where a company was a sham or façade. Anti-avoidance rules are the tax version of that idea, written into statute.

Recap

Planning uses the choices the law offers. Avoidance uses the letter of a rule against its purpose and invites anti-avoidance rules. Evasion depends on concealment and is a crime. Ask whether the plan has a real commercial purpose, and whether it works with every document on the table.

Next: Ford, with Cole, Failure Forensics on two Canadian anti-avoidance cases, Canada Trustco and Deans Knight.
checklist: Classify every tax proposal as planning, avoidance or evasion before discussing its numbers
Write the non-tax commercial purpose of each plan in one sentence
Ask: would this still work if the tax authority saw every document?
Check whether a specific or general anti-avoidance rule targets the technique
Decline any deal that depends on cash without an invoice, and record that you declined
Get a written opinion from an adviser not paid on the size of the saving
Verify every rate, rule and penalty against the primary source for that year

Tax evasion — illegally reducing tax by concealment, false statements or deliberate failure to report

hostile.q: Your structure saves a lot of transfer tax by buying shares instead of land. Why isn't that avoidance?
hostile.a: It may be, and that is why we asked. The share purchase has a commercial purpose we can document: the company holds the approvals and contracts we need, and moving them would cost time and money. Our adviser has checked the land-rich company rules in that jurisdiction and confirmed in writing how they apply, and the model shows the result if transfer tax is payable anyway. If the saving were the only reason, we would buy the land.

title: Canada Trustco and Deans Knight: where the purpose line falls
summary: Two Supreme Court of Canada decisions, eighteen years apart, show where avoidance stops being acceptable. In Canada Trustco in 2005, a sale-leaseback survived the general anti-avoidance rule; in Deans Knight in 2023, a carefully engineered use of tax losses did not. The difference was purpose, and the evidence of it.
rule: Rule 24: No tax plan goes ahead unless I can state its commercial purpose in one sentence and would be content to hand every document to the tax authority on the first day.
body:
Mr Shabazz, two cases from the same court show the same rule giving opposite answers. In one, a tax-motivated transaction survived because it used the rules the way they were meant to be used. In the other, a transaction that obeyed the letter of the rules failed because it achieved exactly what those rules existed to stop.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between tax avoidance and tax evasion?

A. Avoidance uses the words of a rule against its purpose, with real and disclosed transactions; it invites anti-avoidance rules but is generally not a crime. Evasion relies on concealment or falsehood and is a crime.

Q. What is phantom income?

A. Taxable profit allocated to an owner who received no cash to pay the tax, often because the cash went to non-deductible loan principal.

Q. What is appraiser bias, and how do you guard against it?

A. The tendency of an appraisal to drift toward the number the client hopes for. Guard against it by giving the appraiser the full facts, reading the comparables yourself and testing the value with a second approach.

Why this matters

Real estate is full of tax-motivated features: depreciation, losses during development, choice of vehicle, timing of sales. A developer will be offered structures that rely on these features in ways their designers call efficient. These two cases show how a court decides whether efficient has become abusive. Cole sits in because, in both, the outcome turned on what the transactions actually did and on the record of why they were done. The broad facts here are drawn from the published judgments; verify the detail against them before relying on it, and note that the rule itself has since been amended, so check its current text.

Step 1: Timeline

Canada Trustco. In the late 1990s, a financial institution bought a large fleet of truck trailers and leased them back to the seller, in a sale-leaseback largely financed by borrowed money and with arrangements that substantially protected the institution from risk. It claimed capital cost allowance, Canada's system of tax depreciation, on the purchase price. The tax authority applied the general anti-avoidance rule and denied the deductions. In 2005 the Supreme Court of Canada held, unanimously, that the rule did not apply.

Deans Knight. In the late 2000s, a company with large unused tax losses and no viable business entered an arrangement with an investor. The investor obtained substantial economic interest and influence, and a new business was brought into the company, while the arrangement was structured so that there was no legal acquisition of control, the event that would have restricted use of the losses. The Tax Court found for the company, the Federal Court of Appeal reversed, and in 2023 the Supreme Court of Canada, by a majority, held that the general anti-avoidance rule applied and the losses could not be used.

Step 2: Key decisions

In Canada Trustco the key decision was to rely on the depreciation rules as written, on a real purchase at a real price. In Deans Knight the key decision was to engineer the transaction to stop just short of the legal trigger for a specific anti-avoidance rule while achieving the result that rule was designed to prevent.

Step 3: Assumptions

Both taxpayers assumed that obeying the words of the statute was enough. In Canada Trustco that assumption held, because the court found the depreciation rules were meant to apply to cost as defined, and the cost was real. In Deans Knight it failed. The court held that the purpose of the loss-restriction rule was to stop losses being used by a company whose owners and business had in substance changed, and that the arrangement achieved that change by a route deliberately designed to avoid the words.

Step 4: Incentives

In both cases, the tax value of the deductions or losses was the reason the transaction was worth doing. That is not, by itself, fatal. The courts accepted that taxpayers may arrange their affairs to reduce tax. But in Deans Knight the losses were the main asset the company had, and an asset whose only value is a tax benefit is a warning sign in itself.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

In the second case, the warning sign was the precision of the design. When a structure is built to land a fraction short of a statutory line, for example just below a percentage of shares that would count as control, while giving the outsider the practical benefits of control, it is announcing that it knows where the line is and why it exists. Courts read that precision as evidence of purpose.

Step 6: Point of no return

For tax, the point of no return is the moment the transactions are executed. After that, the facts exist and the only question is how a court will characterise them. Opinions obtained later cannot change what was done, or what the contemporaneous documents say about why.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause of the failed plan was treating the statute as a set of words to be navigated rather than a set of purposes to be respected. The Supreme Court's framework, set out in Canada Trustco, asks three questions: is there a tax benefit, was the transaction an avoidance transaction undertaken mainly for that benefit, and does it misuse or abuse the object, spirit and purpose of the provisions relied on. Both cases had the first two. Only one had the third.

The developer's version

This is a hypothetical composite, not either case. A development company carries 5,000,000 of losses from a failed project. A promoter proposes that a profitable investor take a large economic interest in the company through convertible instruments that stay just below the threshold for an acquisition of control, then move a profitable rental portfolio into the company to use the losses. Every document is carefully drafted. The investor's purpose, stated in its own board paper, is "access to tax attributes." That sentence is the case against it.

Cole's evidence check

Cole's point: courts decide purpose from the documents written at the time. Board papers, investment memos, emails, the promoter's marketing deck and the order in which steps were taken all speak. If the only reason given anywhere is tax, and the steps were arranged to avoid a specific rule, expect the purpose to be found. If the commercial reason is real and documented, and the tax rules are applied as they were plainly meant to apply, the transaction is far stronger.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a plan that is legally precise and purposively hollow. The control is Rule 24: a one-sentence commercial purpose, written before the plan proceeds, and a willingness to put every document in front of the authority. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser independent of the promoter, in writing, and a tax litigator's view on any plan that relies on staying just below a statutory threshold.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the first case as permission. Canada Trustco is often quoted as proof that the general rule rarely applies. It is better read as proof that the rules apply as intended, and Deans Knight as proof of what happens when they are not.

Rule 24

Rule 24: No tax plan goes ahead unless I can state its commercial purpose in one sentence and would be content to hand every document to the tax authority on the first day.

Callback

Two lessons ago, in week 22, Fundy Settlement turned on where decisions were really made. Here, the cases turned on why transactions were really done. Both are courts reading conduct and documents rather than labels. And in week 21, the corporate veil was pierced only where a company was a façade. A transaction built to sit just short of a statutory trigger is a façade of a different kind.

Recap

Canada Trustco survived because the depreciation rules were used as intended on a real cost. Deans Knight failed because the loss rules were avoided by a design that achieved what they existed to stop. Tax benefit, avoidance transaction, abuse: the third question decides. Rule 24 is the prevention.

Next: Roman, The Money, on what an aggressive plan really returns once reassessment, interest and penalties are priced.
checklist: Write the commercial purpose of any tax plan in one sentence before it proceeds
Ask which statutory rule the plan is designed to stay just short of, and why that rule exists
Read the promoter's own marketing materials as a court would
Check that board papers state real commercial reasons, not tax attributes
Treat an asset whose only value is a tax benefit as a warning sign
Get an independent written opinion, and a litigator's view on threshold plans
Verify the current text of the anti-avoidance rule before relying on old cases
head: Field checklist
speak: Two Supreme Court of Canada cases show where the purpose line falls. In Canada Trustco, decided in 2005, a financial institution bought trailers and leased them back, claiming tax depreciation on a real cost. The court held unanimously that the general anti-avoidance rule did not apply, because the depreciation rules were used as intended. It also set out three questions: is there a tax benefit, was the transaction done mainly for it, and does it abuse the purpose of the rules relied on. In Deans Knight, decided in 2023, a company with large losses let an investor take functional control and bring in a new business, while carefully avoiding a legal acquisition of control. The court held that this abused the purpose of the loss-restriction rule. The lesson: a plan built to stop just short of a statutory line announces its purpose. Rule 24: state the commercial purpose in one sentence, and be content to show every document on day one.
terms: Capital cost allowance — Canada's system of tax depreciation on capital property
Avoidance transaction — a transaction undertaken mainly to obtain a tax benefit rather than for a genuine non-tax purpose
Acquisition of control — a change in who legally controls a company, which can trigger rules restricting the use of its tax losses

hostile.q: Our structure stays below the control threshold by a comfortable margin. The words of the statute are on our side. What's the problem?
hostile.a: The words are the start, not the end. If the investor gets the practical benefits of control and the only reason for the design is to keep the losses, a court can find that it abuses the purpose of the loss rule, which is what happened in Deans Knight. I'd need a documented commercial reason for the transaction that stands without the losses, and an independent opinion that addresses the purpose question directly, before I'd sign.

title: What an aggressive tax plan really returns
summary: A tax saving that may be reversed is not a saving; it is a bet with fees, interest and penalties attached. This lesson prices an aggressive plan as an expected value, then shows why expected value understates the damage once lenders, investors and your own balance sheet are counted.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an aggressive tax plan does not save you money. It buys a ticket in a lottery where the prize is the saving, the price is the fees, and losing costs the tax plus interest plus penalties, years later, when you have already spent the money. Price the whole ticket.

Recall

Q. In the Canada Trustco framework, which of the three questions usually decides the case?

A. The third: whether the transaction misuses or abuses the object, spirit and purpose of the provisions relied on. Most tax-motivated transactions have a tax benefit and a tax purpose; abuse is the dividing line.

Q. What is a flow-through entity?

A. A vehicle, such as a partnership in many systems, whose profit is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than in the vehicle itself.

Q. What is the cost approach to valuation?

A. Valuing a property at the cost of replacing it, less depreciation, plus the value of the land. It is most useful for new or special-purpose buildings.

Why this matters

Promoters present the saving. They rarely present the probability of losing it, the interest that runs while you wait, the penalties that may follow, the cost of defending it, or what happens to your relationships with lenders and investors during a multi-year dispute. A developer who prices only the saving will accept plans that are bad bets. All figures below are hypothetical and simplified; every rate, interest charge and penalty must be verified against the primary source and with a qualified adviser before you rely on it.

The plan as a bet

In plain English, an aggressive plan has two outcomes. It survives, and you keep the saving minus the fees. Or it fails on reassessment, and you pay the tax you tried to save, plus interest from the original due date, plus possibly a penalty, plus the fees, plus the cost of the dispute.

The professional framing is expected value: the probability of each outcome multiplied by its result, added together. A worked example, hypothetical. A plan promises to save 1,000,000 of tax. Fees are 150,000 up front. Your independent adviser, asked directly, says the chance of the plan being challenged and failing is about 40 percent. If it fails, you pay the 1,000,000 of tax, plus interest that by the time the dispute ends adds a hypothetical 25 percent, or 250,000, plus a penalty the adviser rates as a real possibility at a hypothetical 25 percent of the tax, or 250,000, plus 200,000 of defence costs. The adviser puts the chance of the penalty, given failure, at one in two.

Outcome A, the plan survives: 1,000,000 saved minus 150,000 fees is a net gain of 850,000. Probability 60 percent.

Outcome B, the plan fails: you saved nothing, you paid 150,000 in fees, 250,000 in interest, 200,000 in defence and an expected 125,000 in penalty, which is half of 250,000. Net result, a loss of 725,000. Probability 40 percent.

Expected value: 60 percent of 850,000 is 510,000. 40 percent of minus 725,000 is minus 290,000. The sum is 220,000. On paper, still positive. That is where most analyses stop, and where they go wrong.

Say that out loud now.

Why the expected value is too high

Four things are missing from the 220,000. The first three can at least be estimated.

First, timing. The saving is spent now. The loss arrives years later, as a single bill, possibly when the project is in lease-up and cash is tight. A loss of 725,000 arriving at the worst moment can force a sale or breach a covenant, which the expected value does not see.

Second, financing. Lenders ask about tax disputes. An open reassessment of 1,500,000 or more, including interest and a possible penalty, sits as a contingent liability in your financial statements and in due diligence. Some lenders will reduce leverage, add reserves or decline. Suppose that during the dispute you refinance a 15,000,000 loan and the lender holds back a reserve of 1,000,000 until the dispute is resolved. At a hypothetical 7 percent cost of capital for that money, two years of the reserve costs about 140,000 of foregone return. Your expected value has shrunk to about 80,000.

Third, investors and reputation. An investor reading a disclosure that the sponsor is in an anti-avoidance dispute will ask what else the sponsor is willing to do. That cost cannot be priced reliably, and it can be the largest of all.

There is a fourth cost that never appears in a spreadsheet: your attention. A contested reassessment means document requests, meetings with advisers, reviews of old emails and decisions you made years earlier, often during the same months you are trying to run the next project. A developer's scarcest resource is focused time, and a dispute spends it without asking.

How it moves a deal's return

A second worked example, hypothetical. A project's equity is 10,000,000 and its forecast after-tax profit over four years is 4,000,000, giving an equity multiple of 1.4. The plan adds 850,000 if it works, taking the multiple to 1.485. If it fails, profit falls by 725,000 to 3,275,000, a multiple of about 1.33. The range of outcomes widens from a single point to a spread of 1.33 to 1.485, and the downside lands at exactly the time investors are expecting distributions. A plan that widens the spread for an expected gain of a few percent of profit is usually a poor trade for a sponsor who depends on investor trust.

How the best do it

Large, well-governed property groups commonly have a written tax risk policy approved by their board. It states the level of tax risk the group will accept, requires a genuine commercial purpose for every structure, prohibits schemes whose main benefit is tax, and requires that uncertain positions be identified, documented and, where required, disclosed. Decisions on significant positions go to a named senior officer, not the deal team. A small developer can copy this in one page: a short policy, a list of positions taken and their risk rating, and a rule that nothing rated high proceeds without independent advice and your personal sign-off.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for the personal balance sheet. A tax saving from an uncertain position is not wealth until the period in which the authority can reassess has passed, and that period itself must be verified for each country and each situation. Until then, record it as provisional and keep enough liquidity outside the project to pay the downside if it arrives. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing only the upside and the fees. The control is a written expected-value sheet for every uncertain tax position, with the probability of failure supplied by an independent adviser in writing, interest and penalties included, and a separate note on financing and investor effects. Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser independent of the plan's promoter.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the adviser's "more likely than not" as near certainty. More likely than not can mean a 45 percent chance of failure. Ask for the number, and ask what the number would be if the authority read every email.

Callback

In week 15 you learned that the internal rate of return can flatter a deal that carries a small chance of a large loss. An aggressive tax plan is that shape exactly. And in week 21, Roman priced a personal guarantee the same way: a promise that costs nothing until it costs a great deal.

Recap

Price a tax plan as a bet: probability of failure, tax, interest, penalty, fees and defence. Then subtract what expected value misses: timing, financing reserves and investor trust. Keep uncertain savings provisional until the reassessment window closes. Usually, the honest number is small, and the downside is large.

Next: Vera, The Rules, on penalties, reassessment windows, voluntary disclosure and the records that decide them.
checklist: Price every uncertain tax position as an expected value, not a saving
Get the probability of failure from an independent adviser, in writing, as a number
Include interest, possible penalties and defence costs in the downside
Add financing effects: reserves, reduced leverage and lender questions
Model the equity multiple in both outcomes, not just the expected one
Keep uncertain savings provisional until the reassessment window has closed
Write a one-page tax risk policy and rate each position against it
head: Field checklist
speak: An aggressive tax plan is a bet, so price it as one. Take a hypothetical plan that saves 1,000,000 for 150,000 of fees, with a 40 percent chance of failing. If it survives, you net 850,000. If it fails, you pay the tax back plus interest, defence costs and an expected penalty, and lose 725,000. The expected value is about 220,000. Now add what that number misses. The loss arrives years later as one bill, perhaps during lease-up. A lender may hold back a reserve while the dispute runs, which can cost more than a hundred thousand. And investors who read about an anti-avoidance dispute start wondering what else you will do. The honest gain is small and the downside is large. Get the probability of failure from an independent adviser as a number, keep uncertain savings provisional until the reassessment window closes, and adopt a one-page tax risk policy.
terms: Expected value — the sum of each outcome's result multiplied by its probability
Reassessment — a revised tax assessment issued by the authority after an original assessment, often with interest
Tax risk policy — a written statement of the level of tax risk an organisation will accept and how positions are approved

hostile.q: Your adviser says this plan is more likely than not to succeed. Why wouldn't I take an expected gain?
hostile.a: Because more likely than not still means a real chance of losing, and the loss arrives with interest and possibly penalties, years later, at a time we don't choose. When I add the financing reserve a lender would hold during a dispute, the expected gain on this plan is small, while the downside is a hit to distributions and to your trust in us. I'd rather take the ordinary planning available and keep the structure clean.

title: Penalties, time limits and the records that decide them
summary: Whether a tax position ends as an ordinary adjustment, a penalty or a prosecution usually depends less on the position than on the conduct and records around it. This lesson covers the kinds of penalty, the time limits on reassessment, voluntary disclosure, and the documents that decide which side of each line you fall on.
body:
Mr Shabazz, two developers can take the same doubtful tax position and end in very different places: one pays the tax and some interest, the other pays penalties and faces a much longer exposure. The difference is usually not the position. It is what they disclosed, when, and what their records show they knew.

Recall

Q. Why is the expected value of an aggressive tax plan usually too high?

A. Because it ignores timing, financing effects such as lender reserves during a dispute, investor trust, and the time a dispute consumes. The loss also arrives years later, at a moment you do not choose.

Q. What is the difference between business income and a capital gain, and who decides?

A. Business income comes from a trade, such as building to sell; a capital gain comes from selling an investment. The facts decide, including intention, holding period, financing and activity, not the label you choose.

Q. What does as-complete value mean?

A. The value a property is expected to have once the planned building is finished, as opposed to its as-is value today.

Why this matters

You will take tax positions that are uncertain, because the law is uncertain and real estate is complicated. That is normal. What you control is the conduct around those positions: whether you sought advice, whether you followed it, whether you disclosed what needed disclosing, and whether your records tell an honest story. Those are the facts that move a dispute from ordinary to serious. The rules differ between countries and change often, so this is a map of concepts; every penalty, time limit and procedure must be verified against the primary source and with a qualified adviser in each country before you rely on it.

Three tiers of consequence

In plain English, when a tax position fails, the consequence escalates with the conduct behind it.

  • Tax and interest. The position was reasonable, honestly taken and disclosed, and the authority or a court simply disagreed. You pay the tax and interest from the date it was originally due. Interest is compensation for the time value of money, not a punishment, though in many systems it is not deductible.
  • Civil penalties. The conduct fell below a standard: careless omissions, repeated failures, or a position taken knowingly or with a reckless disregard of the facts. Many systems impose penalties that scale with the tax involved and the seriousness of the conduct. Some also penalise advisers and promoters who make false statements or design schemes.
  • Criminal liability. Deliberate evasion: false records, concealed income, invented expenses. The authority must generally meet a higher standard of proof, and the consequences can include fines and imprisonment.

The professional framing is that the same tax position can land in any of the three tiers depending on what you knew, what you did and what you wrote down.

Time limits on reassessment

Most systems allow the authority a limited period after the original assessment to issue a reassessment, meaning a revised assessment of tax for a year already assessed. In plain English, the books close after a certain time. The period differs by country and by type of taxpayer, so verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

The crucial point is that the period can extend, often without limit, where the taxpayer made a misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness or wilful default, or committed fraud. In those cases the books may never close. Some systems also extend the period for particular transactions, such as dealings with related non-residents, or where the taxpayer signs a waiver.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer files a return for year one and receives an assessment in the spring of year two. Suppose the normal reassessment period in this system is a hypothetical three years from that assessment. If the position was honestly taken and disclosed, the authority must act before the spring of year five. If the return contained a misrepresentation through carelessness, the authority may be able to reassess in year eight or later. Same tax, same position, a very different length of exposure. For your balance sheet, it means an uncertain saving remains provisional for longer than you think, and possibly forever, unless your conduct was clean.

Say that out loud now.

Disclosure, before and after

Two kinds of disclosure matter. Disclosure at the time means telling the authority about an uncertain position when you file, by a note on the return or a separate filing. In many systems certain types of transaction, often those with features typical of aggressive planning, must be reported, with penalties for failing to report; check the current rules. Disclosure at the time does not make a weak position strong, but it can protect you against penalties and against the extended reassessment period, because it is hard to say you hid what you reported.

Disclosure afterwards means coming forward on your own initiative to correct an error or omission before the authority finds it. Many authorities run a voluntary disclosure programme under which a taxpayer who corrects past non-compliance before any enforcement action may receive relief from some penalties or from prosecution, while still paying the tax and usually interest. The conditions are strict: typically the disclosure must be voluntary, complete and made before the authority has started inquiries. Verify the current conditions with the authority's own guidance and an adviser before relying on it.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A developer discovers that a former bookkeeper recorded 200,000 of personal expenses as project costs over three years. If he waits and the authority finds it on audit, he faces the tax, interest and very possibly penalties for gross negligence, and his credibility on every other position is damaged. If he discloses voluntarily and completely before any contact from the authority, he pays the tax and interest and may obtain relief from penalties. The cost of waiting is not only money; it is the authority's view of every other number he files.

The records that decide

Vera's rule is that a contemporaneous record, meaning a document made at the time of the event it records, is worth more than any explanation written later. For a tax position, the decisive records are: the advice you received, with its date and the facts the adviser was given; the board or owner decision approving the position; working papers showing how the figures were calculated; correspondence about the commercial reasons for the transaction; and the disclosure, if any. Keep them together, in one file per position, for longer than the longest plausible reassessment period.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an uncertain position taken with no advice on file, no disclosure and a thin record, because that combination converts an arguable position into apparent carelessness. The control is a tax position file for every uncertain item: the facts given to the adviser, the written advice, the decision, the calculation and the disclosure. Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser in each country, and a tax lawyer before any voluntary disclosure.

The beginner's mistake

Hoping a mistake will not be found. Hope keeps the books open. Correction, made voluntarily and completely, is usually cheaper and always more credible.

Callback

In week 22, Cole showed that residence cases are won on board minutes, emails and travel records. Today the same documents decide whether a doubtful position costs interest or penalties, and whether the books ever close. And on Day 2 this week, the courts in Deans Knight read purpose from the documents written at the time. Records are not administration; they are the evidence that decides the outcome.

Recap

Failed positions escalate from tax and interest, to civil penalties, to criminal liability, according to conduct. Reassessment periods can extend indefinitely for carelessness or fraud. Disclose uncertain positions when required, correct errors voluntarily and completely, and keep a contemporaneous file for every uncertain position.

Next: Nadia, The Numbers, reverse engineering a reassessment notice back to the deduction that caused it.
checklist: Open a tax position file for every uncertain item, with advice, decision, calculation and disclosure
Give the adviser all the facts in writing, and keep a copy of what you gave
Check whether any transaction must be reported to the authority, and report it
Find out, for each country, how long the reassessment period is and what extends it
Correct any discovered error promptly, with a tax lawyer's advice on voluntary disclosure
Never alter or recreate a record after the event
Keep position files for longer than the longest plausible reassessment period
head: Field checklist
speak: The same tax position can end in very different places depending on your conduct. If it was honestly taken and disclosed and the authority disagrees, you usually pay the tax and interest. If your conduct was careless or reckless, civil penalties may follow. If you concealed or falsified, it can be criminal. Time limits matter too. Most systems give the authority a limited period to reassess, but that period can extend, sometimes without limit, where there was carelessness or fraud. So disclose uncertain positions when the rules require it, and if you discover a past error, consider correcting it voluntarily and completely before the authority finds it, with a tax lawyer's advice. Above all, keep a contemporaneous file for every uncertain position: the facts you gave your adviser, the written advice, your decision, the calculation and the disclosure. Records made at the time decide the outcome years later.
terms: Reassessment period — the time an authority has after an original assessment to issue a revised one, which may extend for carelessness or fraud
Voluntary disclosure — coming forward on your own initiative to correct past non-compliance before the authority acts, often in exchange for penalty relief
Contemporaneous record — a document made at the time of the event it records

hostile.q: You've corrected a deduction from three years ago that your adviser now says was wrong. Why should we believe this was an honest mistake?
hostile.a: Because the file shows it. Here is the advice we had at the time, dated, with the facts we gave the adviser; here is the decision to rely on it; and here is the note we filed with the return disclosing the position. When the adviser changed his view, we came to you with the correction rather than waiting. We will pay the tax and interest, and we have reviewed similar items to make sure there are no others.

title: Working backward from a reassessment notice
summary: Starting from a finished outcome, a hypothetical reassessment notice demanding 1,680,000, this lesson works backward to the tax, the interest, the penalty and the deduction that produced it. A second reverse problem finds the probability of failure at which an aggressive plan stops being worth it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when a large tax demand arrives, the first job is to take it apart: how much is tax, how much is interest, how much is penalty, and which number on which return caused it. Working backward turns one frightening total into a set of separate questions, each of which can be answered.

Recall

Q. What can extend a reassessment period beyond its normal length?

A. Misrepresentation through carelessness, neglect or wilful default, or fraud, and in some systems particular transactions or a waiver signed by the taxpayer. Verify the rules in each country.

Q. What is a gross-up, and how is it calculated correctly?

A. A gross-up increases a payment so that the amount left after tax equals a target. You divide the target by one minus the rate; you never add the rate on top.

Q. Why does an appraisal of as-complete value carry more uncertainty than an as-is value?

A. Because it depends on assumptions about a building that does not yet exist: its cost, its completion date, its rents or sale prices and the market at that time.

Why this matters

A reassessment notice is a number with a story inside it. If you can rebuild the story, you can check the authority's arithmetic, separate the parts you can dispute from the parts you cannot, decide whether to object, and tell your lender and investors exactly what is at stake. On even-numbered weeks we reverse engineer, starting from the answer. Every rate here is hypothetical and simplified, and real interest is usually compounded on a schedule set by law; verify every rate and method against the primary source before you rely on it.

The outcome: a notice for 1,680,000

A hypothetical development company receives a notice demanding 1,680,000 for a year three years earlier. The notice says the authority has disallowed a deduction, added interest and imposed a penalty. Assume, for the exercise, that the tax rate on the company's profit is a hypothetical 25 percent, that interest has run at a simple hypothetical 6 percent a year for 3 years, and that the penalty is a hypothetical 50 percent of the tax, of the kind some systems impose for gross negligence.

Step 1: express everything in terms of the tax

Call the additional tax T. Interest is 6 percent times 3 years times T, which is 0.18 T. The penalty is 0.50 T. The notice total is therefore T plus 0.18 T plus 0.50 T, which is 1.68 T.

Step 2: solve for the tax

1.68 T equals 1,680,000, so T equals 1,680,000 divided by 1.68, which is 1,000,000. The notice is 1,000,000 of tax, 180,000 of interest and 500,000 of penalty. Write the tie-out: 1,000,000 plus 180,000 plus 500,000 equals 1,680,000.

Step 3: solve for the disallowed deduction

Tax is the rate times the extra taxable profit. The extra taxable profit is the deduction disallowed. So the deduction is T divided by the rate: 1,000,000 divided by 0.25, which is 4,000,000. The authority has disallowed 4,000,000 of deductions.

Now you can ask the right questions. Which 4,000,000? Is it one item or several? Is it a timing difference, where the deduction is merely moved to a later year and comes back, or a permanent denial? Timing differences cost interest, not tax. And above all, why is there a penalty?

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: check the authority's arithmetic

Authorities make mistakes too, so rebuild their figures before you accept them. Two checks are worth doing every time. First, the interest: if the law compounds interest daily or monthly rather than simply, the 180,000 in our simplified example would be somewhat higher, so confirm the method and the start date the authority used. A start date one year too early adds a whole year of interest. Second, the rate: confirm that the authority applied the rate in force for that year and that entity, not a current or default rate. A difference of a few points on 4,000,000 of profit is tens of thousands of dollars. Errors found this way are the easiest part of any dispute to win, because they are arithmetic, not argument.

Step 5: what the penalty tells you

The penalty is 500,000 of the 1,680,000, nearly 30 percent of the total. It is also the part most driven by conduct, which is the part your records can contest. If the company can show the position was taken on written advice, given all the facts, and disclosed on the return, it may be able to argue that the penalty conditions are not met. Remove the penalty and the total falls to 1,180,000. Remove the penalty and also show that 1,000,000 of the deduction is merely a timing difference, recoverable next year, and the permanent cost falls further. Taking the notice apart has shown you where the money is and which records matter most.

A second reverse problem: the break-even probability

Now work backward from a decision. A promoter offers a plan saving 600,000 of tax for 90,000 of fees. Your adviser estimates that if the plan fails, you will face interest of 120,000 and defence costs of 150,000, plus a penalty of 300,000 with a one-in-two chance of being imposed. What probability of failure makes the plan worthless in expected value?

Step 1, the gain if it survives: 600,000 minus 90,000 is 510,000.

Step 2, the loss if it fails: fees 90,000, interest 120,000, defence 150,000 and an expected penalty of half of 300,000, which is 150,000. Total 510,000. The tax itself is not counted, because without the plan you would have paid it anyway.

Step 3, set expected value to zero. Call the probability of failure p. Then (1 minus p) times 510,000 minus p times 510,000 equals zero. That gives 510,000 equals 2 p times 510,000, so p equals 0.5.

So the plan is worth doing on paper only if the chance of failure is below 50 percent, and that is before timing, financing reserves and investor trust, which Roman showed on Day 3 can remove most of the remaining margin. If your independent adviser says the chance of failure is around 40 percent, the plan's expected gain is 60 percent of 510,000 minus 40 percent of 510,000, which is 102,000, on a plan that puts 510,000 at risk. That is a thin reward for a large, late, lumpy loss.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reacting to the total on a notice, either by paying it in panic or by fighting all of it on principle. The control is to decompose every notice into tax, interest and penalty, trace the tax to the specific items and years, classify each as timing or permanent, and decide on each part separately with an adviser before any deadline to object. Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser and, before any formal objection, a tax lawyer.

The beginner's mistake

Missing the objection deadline while arguing about the merits. Most systems give a limited time to file a formal objection to a reassessment, and missing it can leave you with no right to dispute even a clear error. Find the deadline on the day the notice arrives, verify it against the primary source, and put it in your calendar before anything else.

Callback

In week 22, Nadia worked backward from a partner's tax bill to the phantom income that caused it, and showed that grossing up means dividing by one minus the rate. The same algebra runs this lesson: express every part of the total in terms of one unknown, solve for it, and tie it out. And in week 17 you reverse engineered a deal's land price from public information. A notice is public information about your own deal; read it the same way.

Recap

A notice of 1,680,000 decomposed into 1,000,000 of tax, 180,000 of interest and 500,000 of penalty, from 4,000,000 of disallowed deductions at a hypothetical 25 percent rate. The penalty is the conduct-driven part your records can contest. Working backward from a plan's numbers found its break-even failure probability: 50 percent, before the costs expected value misses.

Next: Cole, The Room, at the table when a promoter pitches a scheme that sounds too good.
checklist: Find the objection deadline on the day a notice arrives, and diarise it
Decompose every notice into tax, interest and penalty, and write the tie-out
Trace the tax to the specific items, years and deductions disallowed
Classify each adjustment as timing or permanent
Pull the advice, decision and disclosure records for any penalty
Compute the break-even failure probability for any aggressive plan
Never pay or fight a notice in full before decomposing it with an adviser
head: Field checklist
speak: When a tax notice arrives, take it apart before you react. Suppose it demands 1,680,000, with a hypothetical 25 percent tax rate, 6 percent simple interest for 3 years, and a 50 percent penalty. Every part is a multiple of the tax: interest is 0.18 of it and the penalty 0.5, so the total is 1.68 times the tax. The tax is 1,000,000, interest 180,000 and penalty 500,000, and the disallowed deduction is 1,000,000 divided by 0.25, which is 4,000,000. Now ask which items those are, whether any are only timing differences, and whether your records can contest the penalty. Work backward from a decision too. A plan that gains 510,000 if it survives and loses 510,000 if it fails breaks even at a 50 percent chance of failure, before timing, financing and trust costs. And find the objection deadline on day one.
terms: Timing difference — an adjustment that moves a deduction or income to a different year rather than removing it
Notice of reassessment — the authority's formal statement of revised tax, interest and penalty for a past year
Objection — a formal challenge to a reassessment, which usually must be filed within a set time

hostile.q: The authority says you owe 1,680,000. Your lender has seen the notice. How much of that is really at risk?
hostile.a: We've decomposed it: 1,000,000 of tax, 180,000 of interest and 500,000 of penalty, arising from 4,000,000 of disallowed deductions. Our adviser's view is that 1,000,000 of those deductions is a timing difference that reverses next year, and we have the written advice and the disclosure that we believe answer the penalty. We've filed an objection inside the deadline, reserved for the full amount in the meantime, and I'll update you when the authority responds.

title: When the promoter says it is all legal
summary: A scene: a well-dressed promoter presents a structure that will make a development profit almost tax-free. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind his pitch, when to stay silent, and how to leave the room with your reputation and your options intact.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous tax scheme is presented by a confident, likeable person who uses the word legal often and the word purpose never. Your job in that room is not to win an argument. It is to ask five questions, write down the answers, and leave without committing to anything.

Recall

Q. In the reverse-engineered notice, what part of the total was most driven by conduct?

A. The penalty, 500,000 of 1,680,000. It is the part that records of advice, decision and disclosure can contest.

Q. What is a hybrid entity?

A. A vehicle treated as transparent by one country and as a separate taxpayer by another, which can produce double tax, lost credits or mismatches that anti-hybrid rules attack.

Q. What does reverse engineering a deal from public information mean?

A. Starting from known facts, such as a sale price or rent, and working backward to the land price, rent or return the buyer must have assumed, to test whether the market's numbers make sense.

Why this matters

Schemes find developers at the moment they are most tempted: after a big sale, during a large refinancing, or when a partner is pushing for higher distributions. They are usually pitched in person, often by someone introduced through a trusted contact, and often with a deadline. If you have a script for that room, you can listen fully, learn something useful, and decline cleanly. If you do not, you may agree to a next step that is hard to unwind. The scene below is hypothetical, and nothing in it is advice about any real structure.

The scene

A hypothetical promoter, introduced by a friend of a friend, meets you after you have completed a project that produced a 4,000,000 profit. He opens: "Our structure routes the profit through a series of entities in three jurisdictions. It's completely legal, it's been used by many clients, and we have a legal opinion. Your effective tax rate drops to almost nothing. Our fee is 20 percent of the saving. We can only take two more clients this year."

The question behind his pitch

Every element of the pitch is designed to move you toward yes. "Completely legal" addresses your fear of evasion and says nothing about avoidance. "Used by many clients" offers social proof. "A legal opinion" offers authority without saying who wrote it, for whom, or on what facts. A fee as a share of the saving rewards him for the size of the claimed benefit, not for whether it survives. And "only two more clients" is scarcity. You studied these levers in week 3. The question behind the pitch is not "is this legal". It is "what does this structure do apart from reduce tax, and who carries the loss if it fails?"

The lines to say

  • "Thank you. Before we go further, what is the commercial purpose of each entity in the chain, apart from tax?"
  • "Who wrote the legal opinion, who was the client, and what facts and assumptions does it rely on? I'd need to see the whole opinion, not a summary."
  • "Does this structure need to be reported to any tax authority under disclosure rules, and will it be?"
  • "If the authority reassesses, who pays the tax, the interest, any penalty and the defence costs? Is your fee refunded?"
  • "I'll take this to my own adviser, who is independent of you, and come back to you if I want to continue."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

  • "That sounds great, let's start the paperwork." You have just made a decision in his room, on his facts, before your adviser has seen anything.
  • "Nobody will ever find out about these entities." Whatever you mean by it, you have just described the test for evasion out loud, in front of a witness.
  • "Can we backdate the documents to before the sale?" Never. A backdated document is a false record, and it can turn a disputed position into a fraud.
  • "How aggressive is it, really?" It invites a reassuring answer and puts nothing on the record. Ask for the specific risks in writing instead.

When to stay silent

After each question, stop and let him answer fully. Then wait two or three seconds more. Promoters are skilled at filling silence, and the second answer, the one that comes after your silence, is often more honest than the first. Write down what he says, in his words. If he declines to name the author of the opinion, or says the opinion is for the firm and cannot be shared, write that down too. It is an answer.

A worked test, in the room

Apply Day 3 and Day 5 mentally. The saving is said to be almost all of the tax on a 4,000,000 profit. Suppose that tax would be a hypothetical 1,000,000. His fee is 20 percent, or 200,000, payable on implementation, before any authority has looked. If your adviser later says the chance of failure is 50 percent, and failure brings back the 1,000,000 of tax with, say, 300,000 of interest and penalty and 150,000 of defence costs, the plan gains 800,000 if it survives and loses 650,000 if it fails. Expected value: half of 800,000 minus half of 650,000, which is 75,000, before timing, financing and reputation. Meanwhile the promoter's 200,000 is certain. In this example, he gains more from the scheme in expected terms than you do.

Holding your state

The pressure in this room is social, not intellectual. You may feel that asking hard questions is rude, especially when the introduction came through a friend. Keep your voice warm and your questions specific. It is entirely possible to be courteous and to refuse to decide. "I never decide on structure in the first meeting" is a complete answer, and it is true of every serious developer.

Ethics and anti-corruption

The same discipline applies at the other end of a tax dispute. Suppose, hypothetically, that during an audit someone suggests that a payment, a gift or a favour could make a problem go away. The answer is no, immediately and without negotiation, and the conversation is recorded in a note to your lawyer the same day. Offering or paying a bribe to an official is a serious crime in most countries, and many countries also prosecute bribery committed abroad by their own nationals and companies; verify the laws that apply to you with counsel.

Decide this now, not in the room. A developer known to refuse every improper payment is approached less often, gets straighter answers from officials, and keeps the trust of lenders and investors who cannot afford to be associated with corruption. Write your refusal line in your decision journal today.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is agreeing to a first step, such as forming an entity or signing an engagement, before independent advice. The control is a standing rule: no structuring decision in the first meeting, no engagement with any promoter whose fee is a share of the saving without independent written advice, and every pitch recorded in a note. Professional sign-off required: an independent tax adviser and a lawyer in each jurisdiction named in the structure.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing with the promoter about whether the scheme works. You cannot win that argument in his room, on his facts. Ask the questions, collect the answers, and let your own adviser do the arguing on paper.

Callback

In week 3 you studied Cialdini's levers of influence: authority, social proof, scarcity and liking. A scheme pitch typically uses all four in one breath. Naming them as they appear takes away most of their force. And on Day 2 this week, the Deans Knight court read purpose from the documents. Your note of this meeting may one day be one of those documents.

Recap

Ask for the commercial purpose of each entity, the full opinion and its author, the disclosure position and who carries the loss. Never decide in the room, never mention secrecy, never backdate. Price the scheme, and notice when the promoter's gain is more certain than yours. Refuse any improper payment, always.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair on avoidance versus evasion.
checklist: Ask the commercial purpose of every entity in a proposed structure
Ask who wrote the legal opinion, for whom, and on which facts, and read it in full
Ask whether the structure must be disclosed to the authority
Ask who carries tax, interest, penalty and defence costs if it fails
Never decide on structure in the first meeting
Never backdate a document, or discuss keeping anything from the authority
Refuse every improper payment and record the approach with your lawyer the same day
head: Field checklist
speak: When a promoter says a scheme is completely legal, remember that legal on the words is exactly what avoidance looks like. Listen for the influence levers: authority from an unnamed opinion, social proof from many clients, scarcity from limited places, and liking from the introduction. Then ask five questions: what is the commercial purpose of each entity apart from tax, who wrote the opinion and on which facts, must this be disclosed to the authority, who pays if it fails, and is your fee refunded. Stay silent after each answer and write it down. Never decide in the room, never talk about keeping things hidden, and never backdate anything. Price it: if the promoter's fee is certain and your gain is a bet, he may gain more than you do. And if anyone ever suggests a payment to make an audit go away, refuse at once and tell your lawyer the same day.
terms: Contingent fee — a fee calculated as a share of a result, such as a tax saving, which rewards the size of the claim rather than its durability
Social proof — the tendency to treat what others are doing as evidence of what is right
Bribery — offering, giving or receiving something of value to improperly influence an official or a business decision

hostile.q: Everyone in your position uses structures like this. Are you really going to leave a million dollars on the table?
hostile.a: I'm going to leave it on the table until someone independent of you tells me in writing what each entity does apart from tax and what happens if it's challenged. If it survives that review, I've lost a few weeks. If it doesn't, I've avoided a bill with interest and penalties and a conversation with my lenders I never want to have. I'll come back to you once my adviser has read the full opinion.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Avoidance versus evasion: the week in six questions
summary: Six questions on planning, avoidance and evasion, the general anti-avoidance rule, penalties and records, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a hypothetical board minute and fee invoice, and a two-minute boardroom explanation of the week.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week comes down to one test: if any part of a plan only works when the authority does not know the true facts, or only works because it defeats the purpose of the rule it relies on, it is not planning. Today we test that, sit in the auditor's chair, and say the week in two minutes.

Recall

Q. What should you say when a promoter tells you a scheme is completely legal?

A. Ask the commercial purpose of each entity apart from tax, who wrote the opinion and on what facts, whether it must be disclosed, and who carries the loss if it fails, then take it to an independent adviser before deciding anything.

Q. What is the difference between a transfer tax and a value-added tax on real estate, in concept?

A. A transfer tax is charged on the transfer of land, usually on the price, and paid once. A value-added tax is charged on supplies through the chain, with businesses generally able to recover tax paid on their inputs, and its treatment of land and new buildings varies widely.

Q. Why should an appraisal be tested with more than one approach?

A. Because each approach has its own blind spot. Comparing the income, sales comparison and cost approaches exposes an assumption that one approach alone would hide.

Why this matters

This is the week that protects everything else. A developer can build a good building, finance it well and sell it at a fine price, and still lose the result years later to a tax position that failed on purpose or on conduct. The ideas are simple. Applying them under pressure, when the saving is large and the promoter is charming, is the skill.

The six questions

Question 1. What separates planning, avoidance and evasion? Answer: planning chooses among options the law offers; avoidance uses the words of a rule against its purpose, with real and disclosed transactions; evasion relies on concealment or falsehood and is a crime.

Question 2. What does a general anti-avoidance rule do? Answer: it lets the authority deny a tax benefit from a transaction undertaken mainly for that benefit which misuses or abuses the purpose of the provisions relied on. Verify the current text, because these rules are amended.

Question 3. Why did Canada Trustco and Deans Knight end differently? Answer: in Canada Trustco the depreciation rules were applied as intended to a real cost, so there was no abuse. In Deans Knight a design that stayed just short of an acquisition of control achieved what the loss-restriction rule exists to prevent, so the rule applied. Rule 24: state the commercial purpose in one sentence and be content to show every document on day one.

Question 4. Why is the expected value of an aggressive plan usually overstated? Answer: because it leaves out timing, lender reserves during a dispute, investor trust and the time a dispute consumes, and the loss arrives late and in one lump.

Question 5. What decides whether a failed position costs interest, penalties or more? Answer: conduct and records: written advice on full facts, the decision to rely on it, the disclosure, and a contemporaneous file. Carelessness or fraud can also extend the reassessment period, sometimes without limit.

Question 6. A notice demands 1,680,000 at a hypothetical 25 percent rate, 18 percent interest and a 50 percent penalty. What was disallowed? Answer: the total is 1.68 times the tax, so the tax is 1,000,000 and the deduction is 4,000,000. Then decompose it into timing and permanent items, and contest the penalty with your records.

Say that out loud now.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Read these two hypothetical documents as a hostile auditor would. Find what an auditor would challenge before you read on.

"Minutes of a board meeting of ProjectCo, held at the registered office abroad. Present: the nominee director. The director approved the management services agreement with HoldCo, previously agreed by the developer, at a fee of 15 percent of ProjectCo's revenue. The director noted that the agreement reduces ProjectCo's taxable profit. The minutes were signed on behalf of the director and dated the first of January."

"Invoice from HoldCo to ProjectCo: management services, year two, 900,000. No further detail."

What the auditor sees. One: the agreement was "previously agreed by the developer," so the decision was made elsewhere and the meeting merely ratified it, which raises the residence question from week 22. Two: the only reason recorded for the agreement is that it reduces taxable profit. There is no commercial purpose on the record. Three: a fee set as a percentage of revenue, with no link to the services actually provided, invites the question of whether the price is what unrelated parties would agree. Four: the minutes were signed on behalf of the director, not by him, and dated the first of January, a date that may not match when anyone met. Five: the invoice describes no services, no hours, no deliverables and no people. An auditor will ask what was done, by whom and where, and will expect evidence beyond the invoice. Six: nothing shows that the structure was reported where reporting might be required. A hostile reader would treat this file as evidence of avoidance at best.

The week on one page

QuestionWhat decides itThe trap
Planning or avoidance?Whether it respects the rule's purposeBelieving the words are enough
Avoidance or evasion?Whether it depends on concealmentThinking secrecy is a privacy choice
Is it worth it?Expected value plus timing, financing and trustPricing only the saving
How bad if it fails?Conduct, disclosure and recordsHoping the error is never found

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to an investment committee. Set a timer. Then compare with this model answer.

"Our tax policy is one page. We use the choices the law offers and nothing that depends on defeating a rule's purpose or on the authority not knowing the facts. Every structure has a commercial purpose we can state in one sentence, and we would hand every document to the authority on the first day. Uncertain positions are priced as bets, including interest, penalties and the financing effects of a dispute, using an independent adviser's probability in writing. Each uncertain position has a file: the facts we gave the adviser, the written advice, the decision and any disclosure. We report what must be reported. We refuse any improper payment. And we treat uncertain savings as provisional until the reassessment period has closed."

Scoring your boardroom answer

Score yourself 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: did you state any rate or penalty as fact? Structure: did you move from policy to pricing to records? Composure: did you slow down at the hard part? The hard question: did you say what you would refuse before anyone asked? Record it on your phone and listen once.

The biggest risk

Passing this quiz and then letting a deal team, a partner or a promoter run the tax decisions. The control is to make the tax risk policy yours, signed, and to review every uncertain position personally at each funding gate.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking a tidy file can rescue a hollow structure. Records prove substance; they cannot create it.

Callback

In week 22 you learned to answer who taxes, what kind of profit and through whom before looking at a rate. This week added a fourth question: is the answer you want consistent with the purpose of the rules? And in week 21, the corporate veil held only for companies run as real businesses. Tax structures are the same: real purpose, real conduct, real records.

Recap

Planning, avoidance, evasion. Purpose decides avoidance; concealment decides evasion. Price uncertain positions honestly, keep records made at the time, disclose what must be disclosed, and refuse every improper payment.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, one test. If a plan only works when the authority does not know the facts, it is evasion, and that is a crime. If it only works by defeating the purpose of the rule it relies on, it is avoidance, and general anti-avoidance rules exist to deny it. Planning uses the choices the law offers. Canada Trustco survived because the depreciation rules were used as intended; Deans Knight failed because a design built to stay just short of a control rule achieved what that rule exists to stop. Price any uncertain plan as a bet, including interest, penalties, lender reserves and investor trust, with an independent adviser's probability in writing. Conduct and records decide whether a failed position costs interest or penalties, and carelessness can keep the books open for years. Keep a file for every uncertain position, disclose what must be disclosed, and refuse every improper payment.
terms: Ratification — approving afterwards a decision already made elsewhere, which can show where real decisions happen
Arm's length — the terms unrelated parties, each acting in its own interest, would agree
Uncertain tax position — a position on a return that the authority could reasonably challenge

hostile.q: Your project company pays its parent 15 percent of revenue for management. Show me what the parent actually did for that money.
hostile.a: Here is the services agreement, the description of each service with the people who delivered it and where, the time records, and the benchmarking our adviser prepared to show the fee is in the range unrelated parties would agree. If any year's records fall short of that standard, we will adjust the fee for that year ourselves rather than defend it.
